The proposed IR stealth scheme uses inverse distance weighted contrast radiant intensity (CRI) to synchronize object and background IR signals.
Repulsive particle swarm optimization (RPSO) is employed to estimate the optimal IR stealth surface temperature.
The test plate used was aluminum with white paint emissivity of 0.82 and dimensions 1000 mm × 1000 mm × 5 mm.
IR stealth performance was tested in midwavelength infrared (3.7–5.1 μm) and longwavelength infrared (7.5–9.1 μm) bands.
Background IR images were captured in a forest scene at approximately 0.4 km distance.
The inverse distance weighted method reduced CRI by up to 91% in MWIR and 79% in LWIR bands.
Compared to the previous area average method, the proposed method improved stealth performance by up to 20% in MWIR and 44% in LWIR.
The previous area average method assumes a constant IR stealth temperature, which limits performance when background IR signals vary.
The IR signal detected by the sensor includes self-emitted thermal radiation, reflected solar/sky irradiance, and atmospheric path radiance.
MODTRAN software was used to model atmospheric transmittance and path radiance based on measured weather data.
The RPSO algorithm updates surface temperature estimates by considering local and global best solutions and random perturbations.
The inverse distance weighting emphasizes background pixels closer to the object, improving stealth effectiveness in heterogeneous backgrounds.
The contrast radiant intensity (CRI) is defined as the weighted difference between object and background IR radiance.
The study was supported by Korean Defense Acquisition Program Administration (DAPA), Agency for Defense Development (ADD), and Chung-Ang University.
Experimental results showed better synchronization of IR signals using the proposed method across three different object positions.
The projected area of the object in the IR image is used in calculating the weighted CRI.
The fitness function in RPSO is based on minimizing the inverse distance weighted CRI to zero.
The study addresses limitations of passive IR detection by actively controlling the object's surface temperature.
The IR cameras used had 640×512 pixel resolution and fields of view approximately 11°×8°.
The study confirms that active IR stealth technologies can be enhanced by advanced optimization algorithms like RPSO.
